blocks.text: As he entered he almost fell, for there was another step behind the door. “The public is shown very little consideration,” he said. “No consideration is shown at all,” said the court usher, “just look at the waiting room here.” It was a long corridor from which roughly fashioned wooden doors led into the separate compartments of the attic. Although there was no direct admission of light, it was not entirely dark, for some compartments had, towards the corridor, mere wooden lattices, reaching, to be sure, right up to the ceiling, instead of solid plank walls, and through these some light penetrated, and through them one could also see individual officials writing at tables or standing right by the lattice and watching the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were only a few people in the corridor, probably because it was Sunday. They made a very humble impression. At almost regular intervals they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches placed along either side of the corridor. All were shabbily dressed, although most of them, to judge by their expressions, their bearing, the fashion of their beards, and many small details scarcely possible to pin down, belonged to the higher classes. Since there were no coat hooks, they had put their hats under the bench, probably each following the example of the next. When those sitting nearest the door caught sight of K. and the court usher, they rose in greeting, and when those farther along saw this, they thought they too must offer a greeting, so that all rose as the two passed. They never stood quite upright, their backs were bent, their knees crooked, they stood like beggars in the street. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: “How humbled they must be.” “Yes,” said the court usher, “they are defendants, all those you see here are defendants.” “Indeed!” said K. “Then they are my colleagues.” And he turned to the nearest, a tall, slender man whose hair was already almost grey. “What are you waiting for here?” K. asked politely. But the unexpected address threw the man into confusion, which looked all the more painful since he was plainly a man of the world who elsewhere must surely have known how to control himself and would not readily relinquish the ascendancy he had acquired over many others. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked towards the others as though they were obliged to help him, and as though no one could demand an answer of him if this help were not forthcoming. Then the court usher came up and said, to reassure and encourage the man: “The gentleman here is only asking what you are waiting for. Do answer him.” The court usher’s voice, which was probably familiar to him, had a better effect: “I am waiting—” he began, and faltered. Evidently he had chosen this beginning in order to answer the question exactly as it had been put, but could now find no continuation. Some of those waiting had drawn near and stood round the group, and the court usher said to them: “Away, away, keep the corridor clear.” They drew back a little, but not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man who had been questioned had collected himself and answered with even a little smile: “A month ago I made several applications for evidence to be taken in my case, and I am waiting for them to be dealt with.” “You seem to be taking a great deal of trouble,” said K. “Yes,” said the man, “it is my own case, after all.” “Not everyone thinks as you do,” said K., “I, for instance, am also accused, but, as I hope to be saved, I have neither made an application for evidence to be taken nor undertaken anything else of the kind. Do you consider it necessary?” “I do not quite know,” said the man, once more in complete uncertainty; he evidently thought K. was jesting with him, and so, for fear of making some fresh mistake, would probably have preferred to repeat his earlier answer in its entirety, but under K.’s impatient gaze he said only, “as far as I am concerned, I have made applications for evidence to be taken.” “You do not believe, I suppose, that I am accused,” K. asked. “Oh, certainly, I beg your pardon,” said the man, stepping a little to one side, but there was no belief in his answer, only fear. “So you do not believe me?” K. asked, and, unconsciously prompted by the man’s humble manner, took him by the arm as though he meant to force him to believe. He had no wish to hurt him and had only touched him very lightly, yet the man cried out as though K. had seized him with red-hot pincers instead of two fingers. This ridiculous crying finally exhausted K.’s patience; if the man did not believe he was accused, so much the better; perhaps he even took him for a judge. And now, in farewell, he did indeed grip him more firmly, thrust him back on to the bench, and walked on. “Most defendants are so sensitive,” said the court usher. Behind them almost all those waiting were now gathering round the man, who had already ceased crying out, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. A guard was now coming towards K., chiefly recognizable by a sabre whose scabbard, to judge at least by its colour, was made of aluminium. K. marvelled at this and even reached out to touch it. The guard, who had come because of the cries, asked what had happened. The court usher tried to reassure him with a few words, but the guard declared that he must nevertheless go and see for himself, saluted, and walked on with very hurried but very short steps, their length probably determined by gout.
